summary: A landlocked country in central Europe in the Alps, known for its long-standing neutrality, direct democracy, multilingual culture, and its watch and finance industries.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has grown rapidly in Switzerland, from about 1% in 1970 to over 30% in the 2020s, making it the largest category. Most Swiss cantons still levy a church tax, and many people formally leave the church to avoid paying it; in addition, postwar prosperity, the spread of education and urbanization, and church sexual-abuse scandals have all accelerated secularization. In cities such as Basel and Geneva, the proportion of non-religious people is even higher.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism has always been an important religion in Switzerland. During the 16th-century Reformation, the central cantons of Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz and others held to Catholicism and were in conflict with Protestant cantons such as Zurich and Bern, and the Kappel Wars (1529 and 1531) even broke out. In 1847 the 'Sonderbund' formed by the Catholic cantons was defeated in a civil war, and the federal constitution was established in 1848. In the 20th century, immigrants flooded in from Catholic countries such as Italy, Portugal and Spain, and for a time Catholics overtook Protestants as the largest denomination.

ranking.name: Swiss Reformed Church (Protestant)
ranking.description: The Swiss Reformed Church originates from the Swiss Reformation of the 16th century: in 1519 Zwingli began reform in Zurich, and from 1536 Calvin pushed reform in Geneva, which came to be called the 'Protestant Rome'. Cantons such as Zurich, Bern, Basel and Geneva became Protestant regions, and the Calvinism of the Swiss Reformed Church influenced the Netherlands, Scotland and North America. But in recent decades large numbers have left the church, and the Protestant share has fallen sharply.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced mainly through immigration from the 1960s onward, first by workers from Turkey, and then, during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, by large numbers of Muslim immigrants and refugees from Kosovo, Bosnia and North Macedonia. In 2009 a Swiss referendum approved a ban on building new minarets, and in 2021 another approved a ban on covering the face in public places, reflecting social controversy over Islam.

ranking.name: Other Christian
ranking.description: Other Christian groups include the Orthodox, Evangelical Free churches and the Christian Catholic Church. Orthodox Christians are mostly immigrants from Serbia, Macedonia, Greece and Romania; the Christian Catholic Church is a denomination that split from the Roman Catholic Church in the 1870s in opposition to the 'papal infallibility' of the First Vatican Council, and has a certain history in Switzerland.

religion.background: Switzerland was gradually Christianized in the 4th–7th centuries, and medieval monasteries such as the Abbey of St. Gallen were important cultural centers of Europe. During the 16th-century Reformation, Zwingli and Calvin made Zurich and Geneva Protestant centers, while the central mountain cantons remained Catholic, and the religious division led to several civil wars, until the federal state was established after the Sonderbund War of 1847. Industrialization and immigration after the 19th century brought religious mobility, secularization accelerated from the late 20th century, and immigration after the 1960s brought Islam and Orthodoxy, forming today's diverse religious landscape.

language.official: The official languages are German, French and Italian, with Romansh as a partial official language.

ranking.name: German (Swiss German)
ranking.description: German became the main language after the Alemanni moved into northern and central Switzerland in the 5th–6th centuries. The everyday spoken language is Swiss German, a collective name for various Alemannic dialects, which differs greatly from Standard German in Germany, though Standard German is used in writing. Because the German-speaking area includes economic centers such as Zurich, Bern and Basel, more than 60% of the population use German as their main language.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French is spoken in the Romandy region of the west, including Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura; this area originally spoke Franco-Provençal dialects, which were gradually replaced by Standard French in the 19th–20th centuries. As the seat of international organizations, Geneva is the most important city of the French-speaking area, and French speakers make up about 23%.

ranking.name: Italian
ranking.description: Italian is spoken in the southern canton of Ticino and in some valleys of Graubünden. Ticino was taken from the Duchy of Milan by the Swiss Confederation in the 15th–16th centuries and became an independent canton in 1803. In the latter half of the 20th century large numbers of Italian immigrants came to work across Switzerland, so Italian also has quite a few speakers in the German- and French-speaking areas.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English is not an official language of Switzerland, but because of globalization, the concentration of international corporate headquarters, and large numbers of foreign professionals from English-speaking and other countries, English is widely used in business and technology in cities such as Zurich, Geneva and Basel. Swiss people from different language regions sometimes also use English as a language of communication among themselves.

ranking.name: Romansh
ranking.description: Romansh is a Romance language descended from Vulgar Latin, spoken in the mountains of Graubünden since Roman times, with five main dialects. Because its speakers are scattered among the valleys, the expansion of German in the 19th–20th centuries gradually caused it to shrink. A referendum in 1938 made it a Swiss 'national language', and in 1996 it gained partial official status, but fewer than 1% have it as their main language.

language.history: The distribution of languages in Switzerland originates in ancient times: in Roman times Latin was used there, and from the 5th century the Germanic Alemanni moved into the north and center, forming the German-speaking area, while the west and south preserved French, Italian and Romansh, derived from Latin. When the Old Swiss Confederacy was founded in 1291, its members were all cantons of the German-speaking area, and it later gradually expanded to the French- and Italian-speaking areas. The 1848 federal constitution recognized German, French and Italian as national languages, and Romansh was added in 1938. Switzerland is known for 'multilingual coexistence'; the cantons decide their own official languages, and schools also require the learning of a second national language.

ranking.name: Fondue
ranking.description: Cheeses such as Gruyère and Vacherin are heated and melted in a ceramic pot with white wine and garlic, and pieces of bread are speared on long forks and dipped in.
ranking.history: Fondue originated among farmers in the Alpine region, and the earliest recipe appeared in a book published in Zurich in 1699. In winter food was limited in the mountains, and farmers heated and melted hard cheese with stale bread to eat. In the 1930s the Swiss Cheese Union promoted cheese fondue as a national dish to increase cheese consumption, and after the Second World War promoted it internationally. Today it has become Switzerland's most representative winter dish and a must-eat for ski holidays.

ranking.name: Raclette
ranking.description: The cut face of a large wheel of raclette cheese is held close to a heat source to melt, and the melted cheese is scraped off over boiled potatoes, pickled gherkins and pickled onions.
ranking.history: Raclette originated among the mountain herders of the canton of Valais, and its name comes from the French 'racler' (to scrape). It is said that as early as the Middle Ages, herders grazing on alpine pastures heated cheese by the campfire and scraped it off to eat. From the mid-20th century, electric raclette grills became widespread, and it changed from food of mountain herders into a dish for family gatherings across the country. In 2007 Valais raclette cheese received protected designation of origin.

ranking.name: Rösti
ranking.description: Grated potatoes are fried in butter into a round cake, golden and crisp outside and soft inside, eaten alone or with fried egg, bacon and sausage.
ranking.history: Rösti was originally the breakfast of farmers in the canton of Bern. Potatoes became widespread in Switzerland only in the 18th century, and because of their high yield they quickly became the farmers' staple. Today it is a national dish, and has given rise to the term 'Röstigraben' (rösti ditch), used as a metaphor for the cultural and political differences between the German- and French-speaking regions, because rösti is regarded as a typical food of the German-speaking area.

ranking.name: Zürcher Geschnetzeltes (Zurich-style sliced veal in cream sauce)
ranking.description: Veal is cut into thin strips and stewed with mushrooms and onions in white wine and cream, with a tender texture, usually served with rösti.
ranking.history: Zürcher Geschnetzeltes is the signature dish of Zurich, and the earliest recipe appeared in a cookbook in 1947. It reflects the food culture of Zurich as a commercial center and middle-class city, using relatively upscale ingredients such as veal, cream and mushrooms. Today it is a classic dish in traditional Swiss restaurants, and serving it with rösti is the most standard way.

ranking.name: Birchermüesli (Swiss oat muesli)
ranking.description: Rolled oats are soaked in milk or yogurt and mixed with grated apple, lemon juice, nuts and honey, with a refreshing taste, usually eaten for breakfast.
ranking.history: Birchermüesli was invented around 1900 by the Swiss physician Maximilian Bircher-Benner, who ran a sanatorium in Zurich and believed that fresh fruit and vegetables were beneficial to health, using them as a dietary therapy for his patients. It is said to have been inspired by food eaten by herders that he encountered while hiking in the Alps. In the late 20th century it became a globally popular healthy breakfast, and the word 'müesli' entered many languages.
